groups.name: thegentlemen
groups.about: The Gentlemen is a ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in July–August 2025 and quickly claimed over 320 victims in 17+ countries. It offers affiliates a 90% revenue share and uses a Go-based locker against Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD. A 2026 compromised C2 server revealed over 1,570 linked victims.

groups.name: qilin
groups.about: Qilin ransomware was first observed in July 2022. It is written in Golang and offers multiple encryption modes that the operator controls. The group uses double extortion, demanding payment for a decryptor and for not releasing stolen data.

groups.name: incransom
groups.about: INC Ransom is a prolific ransomware-as-a-service operation active since July 2023. It targets healthcare, government, education, and manufacturing in North America and Europe, with no sector excluded. It posted over 200 victims in 2025 alone.

groups.name: silentransomgroup
groups.about: Silentransomgroup is described in the notes as a former Conti team, also tracked as Chatty Spider and UNC3753. The notes give no further details on its operations or targets.

groups.name: safepay
groups.about: SafePay emerged in September 2024 and grew rapidly while rejecting the RaaS model, running all operations in-house. It claimed over 300 victims worldwide by mid-2025. An early high-profile attack on UK telematics firm Microlise reportedly stole 1.2 TB of data.

groups.name: akira
groups.about: Akira reportedly emerged in March 2023 and has been speculated to have ties to the former Conti group. Its affiliates reportedly also work with Snatch and BlackByte. The first version was written in C++ and later versions in Rust. Initial access has involved brute-force attacks on Cisco VPNs and exploitation of two CVEs.

groups.name: rhysida
groups.about: Rhysida is a ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in May 2023. It uses phishing and Cobalt Strike to breach networks and deploy its payload. It threatens to publish stolen data, leaves PDF notes, and accepts Bitcoin. The notes say the ransomware is still in early development.

groups.name: medusalocker
groups.about: The notes describe Medusa as a DDoS bot written in .NET 2.0, not a ransomware group. Its current command-and-control uses HTTP, while its predecessor used IRC. The notes do not describe ransomware activity, so this entry may be mislabeled.

groups.name: aurora
groups.about: Aurora is ransomware associated with a multi-purpose Go-based malware in use since mid-2022. Multiple criminal teams distribute it, and it is also sold on underground forums as an infostealer and botnet under the same name.

groups.name: braincipher
groups.about: Brain Cipher emerged in July 2024 with both Windows and Linux variants. It reportedly uses a leaked LockBit Black build and is suspected of exploiting CVE-2023-28252. Demands start at $150,000 and are paid in Monero. In 2025 it moved its negotiation portal to a new server.

groups.name: metaencryptor
groups.about: Ransomware group first observed in mid-2023. Targets medium-to-large enterprises in legal, technology, logistics, manufacturing, and finance, mainly in the UK, Europe, and Southeast Asia. Uses AES-256 and RSA-2048 encryption with double extortion.

groups.name: everest
groups.about: Everest collects and analyzes information about its victims, focusing on customer privacy, financial data, databases, and credit card information. It leaks stolen data on the darknet. It threatens to leak data and keep victims' files if they do not make contact.

groups.name: lockbit5
groups.about: LockBit 5.0, also called ChuongDong, emerged in September 2025 after the February 2024 law enforcement takedown of LockBit. It introduced cross-platform payloads targeting Windows, Linux, and VMware ESXi. It continues the RaaS affiliate model of its predecessors.

The agent probed the infrastructure, went away for 11 hours, then came back with an exploit.

Timing how long the exploit code took to run is absolutely ridiculous.

To make an analogy: it's like someone writing an essay, timing how long it took them to physically hand it in to the professor, then saying "completing the essay took 1.3 seconds".

While technically correct (the essay was not completed until it was handed in). Any reasonable person is going to thinking "completing an essay" means from start to finish.

AI can do some tasks very fast. But these types of metrics are intentionally misleading. They're designed to spread FUD and delude people about how fast AI attacks actually are.

ARTEX did not hack the admin account in 1.3 seconds. ARTEX spend 11 hours developing attack tools and one of the tools took 1.3 seconds to run (that's actually fairly slow for code, but not unreasonable).

The point of focus should be that the AI was able to weaponize a vulnerability in 11 hours (it would likely take a human much longer), not that the exploit took 1.3 second to run (it would take a human the exact same amount of time).

Imagine for a second, if I had personally stopped what would have been the largest cyberattack in history. One that would have erased millions upon millions of computer systems, and the damage that it did do made ARTEX look like a children's toy. 

In that hypothetical reality, I might have some informed opinions on how likely is it that *insert boogeyman of the year* is going to drastically change the cybersecurity landscape, or whether people will just go back to not caring about security in a couple of months time when it's old news.

You can tell who doesn't work in cybersecurity, because they're convinced it's a great time to be in the industry because "more cyberattacks means more cybersecurity spending".

It's a great time to be a shareholder, and that's about it. 

I am not aware of a single company that operates on the basis of "cyberattacks are up 10%, we need to hire 10% more defenders".

What actually happens, is 10% more cyberattacks means 10% more work for the same pay. And the workload just keeps increasing until people end up burning out and quitting, or worse.

At some point if things get bad enough, a company may, and that is a very heavy lifting "may", find budget for additional headcount.

But, like, go find me someone who works in cyber defense and isn't burnt out, and I'll find you someone who doesn't do any work.

Cybersecurity is one of those industries where IMO the salaries only look good on paper. 

If you're coming from a minimum wage customer service job, it's definitely a huge improvement. But if you're going into white collar work anyway, there's so many jobs that pay well and won't burn you out.

digest.overview: Active exploitation of network flaws, trojanized Windows software, AI-agent-driven intrusions, and a string of breaches at major firms and agencies dominate the feed.

themes.title: Exploited and unpatched network device flaws
themes.summary: Juniper Session Smart Conductor flaw is reported as exploited in attacks. A separate Cacti zero-day has a public proof-of-concept giving remote code execution and no patch. The posts do not name CVE IDs, so verify affected versions and mitigations before acting.

themes.title: Breaches at SAP, US Air Force cloud, FIFA
themes.summary: SAP confirmed a cybersecurity incident, and two outlets report that source code may have been compromised. A US Air Force cloud platform was reportedly hacked in a latest federal breach. FIFA says it was hit by a cyberattack that accessed personal and business information.

themes.title: AI agents used in real intrusions
themes.summary: Unit 42 reports more than ten campaigns in which attackers deployed autonomous AI agents through web shells, compressing timelines from days to hours with standard tools. Switzerland confirmed AI agents helped hackers breach two critical infrastructure operators, with four of five AI-assisted attacks succeeding.

themes.title: Consumer and health data breaches
themes.summary: pCloud confirmed a password manager hack after suspicious login alerts. Boston Scientific disclosed a breach exposing personal and medical information. A Colorado breach affected about 100,000 people, and Hex Package Manager warned of a potential data breach.

themes.title: Trojanized Windows downloads and store apps
themes.summary: Hackers poisoned official Q-Dir and DesktopOK downloads and updates to install remote access malware, while the tools still run normally. Separately, a Microsoft Store app named Setup Assistant was used to deliver Vinci RAT, and Microsoft reportedly dismissed the initial abuse report.
